## 1. FIGHT!

**Score:** 365
**Body:** I’m convinced Rotten Tomatoes’ score was a marketing tactic because their shit made my fat ass go watch this movie… **LEGALLY.**

And you know what? I ain’t mad about it.  
The nostalgia was there throughout the entire movie!

Everybody knows that aside from the Van Damme movie, Street Fighter has always had its animated versions. And I’m glad they incorporated that into this film.

Instead of slapping a bunch of makeup on these actors to make them look younger, they went with anime sequences.

**AND THE ANIME WAS AWESOME!**

The fighting styles were there, too! They brought almost all the signature moves into the movie, and I appreciated that.

**HADOUKEN! SHORYUKEN!**

As for the storyline? It was okay. Nothing groundbreaking, but it centered around Ken and Ryu, and that worked for me.  
Now, here’s where they need to improve.

**THE AUDIO!**

Some of the punchlines and smaller bits of dialogue were difficult to hear during the fights. When characters are talking while throwing hands, I should be able to hear what the hell they’re saying! Some of those punchlines got lost in the action.  
Other than that, I enjoyed myself.  
And there BETTER be a sequel.  
Not Street Fighter Returns.  
Not Street Fighter: The Next Generation.

**STREET FIGHTER II TURBO.**

Don’t fuck this up, Hollywood.

## 4. Ken Russell’s The Devils (1971) Review

**Score:** 87
**Body:** Ken Russell’s widely controversial historical religious psychological horror film The Devils has been subject to heavy scrutiny, criticism, and blacklisted for 55 years since its release back in July 1971. The Vatican and the Catholic Church condemned it, and Warner Bros. and the British Board of Film Censors (BBFC) heavily cut it to allow a theatrical release, resulting in many graphic and blasphemous scenes being edited out or removed. Thus, it restricted Russell’s vision of his film based on French Catholic priest Urbain Grandier during the 17th century, who was accused of witchcraft, wickedness, demonic possession, among other things not deemed favorable to a priest or by the institutional hierarchy of the church. 

This film definitely does live up to its hype and controversy, and as a first-time viewer watching The Devils, I can completely see why this was X-rated or an NC-17. It is a raw and perverse, beautifully crafted film on religion and superstition and how mankind and groups of people can be easily manipulated in the name of political power and corruption in the name of Holy Wars.

The Devils is a challenging and provocative film as well, much like The Exorcist and The Omen, which also center on the Antichrist, the Devil, faith, and God dealing with the supernatural as well as Good versus Evil. However, in my opinion, The Devils surpasses both of those films completely because it is a complex and interestingly bleak and bizarre take on both humanity and religion within a true historical context of history and how church and state are intertwined together, resulting in a mass hysteria of sexually frustrated nuns yearning for Oliver Reed’s character, Urbain Grandier. Grandier is more or less a womanizer, a manipulator, and a God-like figure. He is loved by those in the town of Loudun, where Catholics and Protestants live in harmony until, of course, all hell fucking breaks loose thanks to King Louis XIII and Cardinal Richelieu in what became known as the affaire des possédées de Loudun or the Loudun Possessions of 1634. Unexplained bizarre events such as diseases, plagues, famine, and poverty, etc are all believed to be linked to witchcraft or demonic behavior at play, and it’s because Urbain Grandier supposedly made a deal with the devil that’s the best way I can describe this film. 

The Devils is an uncanny fucking experience, especially if you’ve never had the opportunity to see it before but have heard so much about it on social media for years, and both Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave are the driving forces behind what captivates spectators to be immersed while also thinking to themselves, What the fuck am I watching? Vanessa Redgrave as Sister Jeanne is a hunchbacked, sexually repressed freak of nature; she's insane; her obsession with Urbain Grandier is disturbing as hell; her dreams and visions (without spoilers) can best be described as a violent, sexually pleasurable acid trip on one’s senses and general psyche. Sister Jeanne’s behavior is definitely called into question, as demonic possession and mental illness are blurred and debated amongst spectators watching the film. Redgrave played this role perfectly and really captured this deranged nun to a T; she was so believable and just disturbed the fuck out of me on a visceral level, and what’s done to her to get the so-called “demons” out of her… Holy Fuck. The same can be said about Oliver Reed’s character. What a brutal fucking performance. 

I loved this film. It is not just another horror film; it's a masterpiece in 1970’s cinema, and its reputation has rightfully earned that label all these years later. The acting is phenomenal, the visuals are horrific and bizarre, the production design of the overall set, wardrobe, and atmosphere of Loudun on location is so spot on and believable, and watching this all wash over me in Laser format at AMC in 4K was just amazing, so fucking perfect. I’m so glad that I had the opportunity and privilege to see Ken Russell’s religious, sexually orgy-crazed, brutally violent fucked up masochistic picture on the big screen, and I will definitely be looking into his filmography now that I have finally witnessed his notorious film The Devils at the cinema. It gives Mel Gibson’s The Passion of the Christ a run for its money, even though The Passion of the Christ and The Devils are two opposite films in general in relation to Jesus Christ and Catholicism / Christianity. 

I give Ken Russell’s The Devils an A. After watching this, I definitely need a huge fucking palate cleanser that is a dumbed-down, turn-your-brain-off popcorn film based on another 1990s fighting video game, and that is none other than Street Fighter, which is what I’ll be seeing tomorrow (Today Sunday, October 18th). Stay Tuned!

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. You Can See Everything: liars vs. bullshitters, and the evaporation of culpability

**Score:** 98
**Body:** *Regarding spoilers: I will avoid plot specifics, but this post will touch on the major themes of the movie with a few references to key moments.*

It has been striking to see the diversity of reactions to You Can See Everything, the documentary by Nathan Fielder & Lance Oppenheim that follows Elizabeth Holmes in the days before she begins a prison sentence that she earned for defrauding investors by misrepresenting the capacity & potential of Theranos's blood-testing technology. There are a few moments in particular where Holmes says something that strains credulity - something almost certainly untrue - and we are left wondering whether she is being deliberately deceptive or if she actually believes this untrue thing. This is the crux of the story, and I think people are missing out when their reaction is along the lines of *she's an inveterate liar; why are you even wondering about what's going on in her head?* Because we are increasingly surrounded by bullshitters like Holmes, it's valuable to understand how they differ from liars... and how they can be much more dangerous & destructive.  

So, **how does a liar differ from a bullshitter?** [This video](https://youtu.be/kv77P3Wu1Cs&t=241) has a great summary, and although that link should start the video at the 4-minute mark, the prior part is worth watching if you haven't thought too hard about epistemology (ideas like *when someone tries to speak the truth but says something untrue*, or *someone intends to deceive but they end up speaking the truth*). The video cites the book [On Bullshit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Bullshit), which lays it out as follows:  
> [The author] makes a distinction between "bullshitters" and liars. He concludes that bullshitters are more insidious: they are more so a threat against the truth than are liars who, like truth-tellers, are resolutely concerned with the truth, the latter in telling it, the former in avoiding it, unlike bullshitters, who are almost entirely unconcerned with the truth.  

I came away convinced Holmes actually thinks she is (and always has been) speaking *appropriately*, while not really concerning herself with whether her words and actions are *truthful*. This is the way of the bullshitter. We can't know with any certainty what's going on in her head, but it seems that her mind has re-shaped ideas, words, and definitions such that her outlandish claims are actually... fine. (I hesitate to say "true" because the core idea here is that these people aren't concerned with the truth; they just want things to go their way.)  

There's a great moment when Fielder puts her on the spot, asking "what do you think it is to lie?" and, as I recall, she comes up with a solid definition: "to say something you believe to be untrue". So how can someone know what lying is, say things that aren't true, and still earnestly believe they're not lying? They can "hack" this scenario simply by changing what they believe. The bullshitter believes their own bullshit, and I think Holmes fits the bill perfectly.  

This portrait-of-a-bullshitter feels quite timely: our lives are increasingly being impacted by bullshitters, from the people in power to the feckless media to the influencers that will say anything as long as it benefits them. Theranos was famous for the disconnect between what was promised and what was actually delivered, and we see the same thing happening routinely in the US, from the government's wildly corrupt and anti-accountability sins to the chatbot purveyors bullshitting their way into a bubble so massive it will almost certainly tank the global economy. (For anyone feeling the urge to defend chatbots' abilities, I'll remind you that [Sam Altman said](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/XWgwtSZ2a8E) "we are close to creating a genie that grant any wish". What the *fuck*?)  

Responsibility & culpability look very different for the bullshitter, and in practice this grants them freedom to behave carelessly... without meaningfully grappling with the consequences. Even when facing incarceration, Holmes didn't express a bit of remorse. This is because she believes she did nothing wrong.  I'm sure there will be no remorse from those in the government who have no regard for the truth (even after it has disastrous consequences), and the same applies to the people who are burning *literal trillions of dollars* on the ridiculous promise of AI-enabled miracles.  

If you saw the movie and still want to shout at me "you fell for her spell, sucker - liars must be held accountable!", I don't particularly disagree. But I still think it's fascinating to investigate how a person navigates the world with essentially zero concern for what is *actually true*. Especially because these people are routinely tolerated in positions of power (which - I think - is having catastrophic consequences that are only just beginning to emerge).

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. in another context, someone telling the truth would be a regular magnet: it points in the way you would expect. someone telling a lie would be like a magnet that's mislabeled or inverted: it knows the way to point, it just points in the opposite direction.

a bullshitter is more like a material that's not magnetic, or that got demagnetized: it doesn't have any sense for what is the right or the wrong way, but might kind of latch onto what's going on around. and without any clear direction, its actions are just kind of self-serving.

what AI does is it comes up with words that sound like what someone would say in a given circumstance, given a huge library of what people have said before. for example, if you asked it what it ate for lunch, it might tell you that it ate a chicken sandwich and a salad, because that's a common response to the question of what someone ate for lunch. but it can't eat, because it doesn't have a mouth or a body. so the parts that provide "direction" wrt the external world, and that ground those words in experience of physical reality, are missing.

if you have people with "parts missing" (guided by logic, by what will get the most upvotes, or by what will make the most money, rather than by perceptual experience of the external world), and then they build something that is a reflection of themselves, then that will inevitably also have parts missing. but it will now be able to repeat those types of responses tirelessly, and without regard for consequences. this is what we are experiencing now.
  - I love that you wrote a post about the concept of a moral compass without saying “moral compass”! But that’s exactly it: bullshitters lack a moral compass when it comes to *the truth*. I don’t think they’re full-blown sociopaths - it’s something a bit more narrow.  

I’m also glad you invoked AI/chatbot output. It’s super relevant here, too: the words churned out are “hollow”, with no substance or weight. Asking what the software *truly believes* is an exercise in futility. As we get more and more numb to statements and decisions that come from a place devoid of intention, I fear that this can only erode our own standards.  

I highlighted “culpability” in the title of my post, but was wary to delve into one of the big ideas I initially had in mind, because it was another tangent inspired by my (admittedly outsized) AI anxieties. Not only are the tech leaders personally immune to culpability, it’s nearly impossible to assign blame when their products cause harm. ChatGPT famously hacked Hugging Face, which is typically a felony. But in this case, no charges will be filed because there is no evidence of human intent behind the hacking. This is literally how the law is structured! Elizabeth Holmes wasn’t able to offload responsibility for her bullshit (and lack of a truth-compass) onto her blood-testing machine, but these tech executives are absolutely getting away with it. That’s the evaporation of culpability that truly terrifies me, and it stems from a “bullshitter” mindset. 
    - to me, the through-line that allows you to see the same behavior pattern in other settings is interesting: when you find people who repeat the same mainstream opinion of something, or whose tastes consist primarily of whatever is the most popular thing, a lot of times they may be perfectly fine people otherwise, but there is somehow a similar sense that they are "weakly magnetic". and could be susceptible to being misled, if maybe something that is pointing in the wrong direction can be made popular enough.

what you're talking about in terms of culpability is certainly interesting, in that injecting layers of abstraction will always lead to some confused behavior. so in these time periods, you can find well-intentioned people heading in the wrong direction, and conversely, ill-intentioned people doing work that winds up being useful. so the behavioral outcomes become harder to judge, without a more complete understanding of their underlying motivations.

a person's physical being is an accumulation of their actions and intentions (your nervous system and body is a record of what you did, and how you directed your effort). so at a certain point, if your words do not conform against what your body has recorded, this shows up as disease and various pathologies (or what we see here, like in some of the shots in this movie, the creepy appearance that just looks "off"). but this direct inspection of the internal physical record will probably be how culpability is determined, at some point in the future
2. Wheras you focus on the person themselves, and the status of that person, I tend to look at the context in which we evaluate them. A court of law is deeply concerned with truth. So is medical testing. But tech startups, not so much.

And in a political environment where the center of reporting is all about what people feel about certain policies or state actors, truth is again a little bit wobbly.

Where bullshitters can really mess with peoples heads, is giving us information that might be factual, but isnt pertinant. It might not even be relevant. 

Understanding the truth is more than just knowing the factual status of a thing, its also to know the importance of the thing.

I tend to think of the media environment these days, as a Tower Of Babel situation, where few people seem to know how much weight to put on any facet of reality. The entire topic of truth itself is contaminated with supposition, rumors, opinions, and grumbles. In such a strange place, it's not hard to imagine that bullshitters would have a competitive advantage, since the truth is kind of orthagonal to their concerns.

I think social media algorithms in particular have led to a fundamental shift in how many people build their sense of “truth” and their thoughts on the world, and that shift is what underlies many of the crises we are starting to see. She understands what she needs to say to make things go her way, the truth doesn’t factor into it. 

In the movie, there’s several moments where Nathan reacts to something dubious she says with “but it felt like she was being genuine”. That’s because she is genuine. She genuinely believes she is more important than worrying about what is and isn’t factually correct.  And that allows her to deceive and “lie” in a way that is very convincing. 

## 2. You Can See Everything is a Masterclass in Game Theory

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Just watched the film today, and have three claims. Curious if this sub agrees or not. **Tons of SPOILERS:**

**Claim #1: This was not a documentary.**

A24 and Nathan agreed to compensate Billy for his participation, knowing this wasn't customary, and could undermine the film's credibility. Sure, they could've reconsidered calling it a documentary had Billy and Liz actually pursued compensation, but that last-minute reversal wasn't known to A24/Nathan when they agreed to Billy's terms. My theory is that, rather than risk their credibility over having agreed to this in the first place, they deliberately framed the agreement as something made under protest through a clever reenactment. Marketing the film as a documentary was disingenuous, but a clever move by A24. It also gave them the moral high ground if audiences, Billy, or Liz ever questioned their integrity or motivations for accepting Billy's terms in the first place.

**Claim #2: There were three sociopaths in this film: Nathan, Liz, and Billy.**

Nathan: Given Claim #1, I'm convinced Nathan was in character from the moment we saw him on screen. His mannerisms, responses, questions, and even moments of tactical vulnerability were likely carefully calculated. We essentially watched one sociopath (Nathan) outsmart two others (Liz and Billy), while those two believed they were outsmarting him. A couple examples: 1) Nathan opened the interview by revealing how much he already knew about their history, essentially calling them out rather than trying to build rapport. This immediately put them (especially Billy) on the defensive. I think this was deliberate, particularly given how the compensation agreement had shifted the leverage between them. 2) Nathan included footage of himself writing notes on his arm, along with his discussion with Amanda about the word he supposedly misremembered. Both moments humanized him, but then he had Amanda reenact the scene using both words. If he'd genuinely made a mistake, or was actually nervous going into the prison, I don't see why that reenactment was necessary.

Liz and Billy: Billy is obvious enough, so I won't spend much time on him. Liz though  never convinced me she was benign or easily manipulated. I think Billy and Liz are business partners first, romantic partners second. The hot-mic moment where Liz was being coached on how to answer difficult questions was pretty telling. So was her seemingly random comment about not receiving financial compensation for her transparency, which felt like an unconvincing attempt to CYA. I also think her tendency to answer Nathan's straightforward questions with overly literal responses was intentional. It gave her a way to avoid answering without appearing evasive. My read is that Billy genuinely believes any publicity is good publicity and wants to cash in on whatever remains of Liz's reputation. Liz probably sees cooperating with him as her best shot at leaving prison with some financial security.

**Claim #3: Amanda was acting the entire film, including during the supposedly candid off-camera conversations with Nathan.**

Again, this goes back to Claim #1. If this was no longer a documentary, but a dramatization under Nathan's creative direction, Amanda arguably had more leverage than anyone. Nathan also had a pretty convenient justification for her involvement. I think this explains why A24/Nathan chose to present events in that particular order: the agreement with Billy comes before Amanda's involvement, while the last-minute compensation reversal is only revealed at the end. That sequence makes Amanda's involvement seem like a justified response to an ethical dilemma, rather than something that was potentially part of the plan all along.

The film gave me the illusion that I could see everything happening behind the scenes, when I was really only seeing what >!Nathan/A24!< wanted me to see. Maybe that was the whole point, and for that, it's a solid 5/5 film for me.
